title: How to check if a company is legit
summary: How to check if a company is legit: confirm it is registered and active, then check its record, history and people. Sixtyfour researches its history and people.
body_markdown:
Look the company up in the official business registry where it says it was formed and confirm it is active, then check that the record matches the name, address and people it gave you. Check that its website and other people's mentions of it are as old as the history it claims, that the people it names exist and work there, and search its name with the words "complaint" and "scam". Contact it through details you found yourself, never only the ones it sent you.


Search the business registry of the state where the company says it was formed, which is usually run by the secretary of state; the National Association of Secretaries of State links to each state's registration pages and name databases. Search the name without its ending, such as LLC or Inc., include inactive records, and read the status, formation date, registered agent and, where the state publishes them, the officers or managers. A company formed in one state can also be registered in another, and the two records can differ.


Search the number in the registry that issued it, such as Companies House in the UK, a US state's business search or Corporations Canada's federal corporation search, and check that the name it returns is the name on your contract or invoice, letter for letter. A real number that returns a different name is a typo or a borrowed number, and either way a question for the company. In the UK, the free Companies House service also shows the company's status, registered office, incorporation date, officers and previous names.


Yes. A registry records what was filed with it: Companies House, for example, checks that every filing is complete and valid, but says a close review of each document during registration "is not always possible". A company can be formed with false details, a dissolved company can be reinstated by someone with no connection to it, and a new company can borrow an older one's history, so the registration is where the checks start.


Look up when the domain was created and compare it with the history the site claims, then look for the company in places it does not control, such as press, directories and the profiles of people who work there. The FTC notes that https at the start of a web address means the site is encrypted, and that this does not make it a legitimate site. Search the company's name with the words "complaint" or "scam", and do not buy from a seller that insists on payment by gift card, wire transfer, payment app or cryptocurrency.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes a company's name and website, researches sources across the web, and returns the answers you ask for, such as when the business first appears outside its own website, what is at its address and who runs it, with the sources behind them and a confidence score. Anything it could not establish is reported as open, and a person on your team decides.


Stop, send nothing more, and if you paid by bank transfer, report it to your bank at once and ask it to reverse the payment. Report the company to the FTC and to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, and keep a record of its name and website, what you ordered or agreed and every message you exchanged.
